articles.title: 'Resign first': Chirag Paswan dares Rahul Gandhi amid SIR stir; criticises police brutality
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Union minister Chirag Paswan on Wednesday challenged Rahul Gandhi to resign before questioning the electoral process, invoking the Congress
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Union minister Chirag Paswan on Wednesday challenged Rahul Gandhi to resign before questioning the electoral process, invoking the Congress leader’s own victory in Raebareli to counter his criticism of the Election Commission.Paswan, however, condemned the use of force against students protesting alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, saying brutality against demonstrators was unacceptable.The remarks came amid ongoing protests in Delhi demanding action against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged voter-roll irregularities and SIR rollback. While opposing police excesses, Paswan cautioned against viewing the clashes from a single perspective, alleging that anti-social elements could infiltrate demonstrations and provoke confrontations under the cover of student protests."I certainly do not condone brutality. I would never support the use of force in this manner against students—or anyone else, for that matter," Paswan said.He, however, cautioned against viewing the incident from one perspective, alleging that anti-social elements sometimes infiltrate protests and use students and young people as cover to provoke confrontations with police."But at the same time, it is also important to understand the circumstances: where it happened, what exactly occurred, and how it unfolded. Because we see visuals from both sides," he said."There are instances where anti-social elements infiltrate the crowd, using students and the youth as a cover. They confront the police—and let’s not forget, police personnel are human beings too; they have families," Paswan added.He said escalation by either protesters or the administration was inappropriate, stressing that the use of force could not be justified merely by provocation."This kind of escalation shouldn't happen on either side," he said. "There are anti-social elements who use such protests as a pretext to spread anarchy. And it is wrong when they raise their hands against the police.""Equally, when the administration takes such harsh action—whether due to provocation or other reasons — that, too, is not appropriate," he added.Paswan also criticised Rahul for repeatedly raising the issue, accusing the Congress leader of politicising the matter. He questioned the LoP's challenge to the electoral process, pointing to the Congress leader's victory from Rae Bareli and his sister Priyanka Gandhi Vadra's victory from Wayanad."Rahul Gandhi often tries to find a political angle in everything," Paswan said, adding, "But to politicize the matter to this extent and repeatedly hold press conferences about it shows that your priorities are not clearly defined.""Resign yourself first—you won from Raebareli based on this very election process; your sister Priyanka won from Wayanad in the same manner; your 99 MPs won through this exact process," he added.Rahul, meanwhile, met students allegedly injured during the protests at Sonia Gandhi’s residence in Delhi’s Janpath on Wednesday. He appealed to Prime Minister Narendra Modi not to obstruct the protesting students, describing them as “the voice of the country”, and assured them that the Congress would stand by them.Rahul also called on students to document evidence of alleged police action, "I also want to tell the police with love that I have asked every student to make videos, keep evidence with them and send it to us. When this entire episode ends, we will get justice and punish those who have beaten up our students, from top to bottom -- from Narendra Modi, Amit Shah, Gyanesh Kumar to all the constables who are raising their hands on our children."Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: A Vermont forester bought 175 acres of degraded woodland in 2017; after nine years of restoring habitats, the land now features a wildlife pond, rich vegetation and an orchard of more than 100 fruit trees
articles.summary: Vermont forester Ethan Tapper bought 175 acres of degraded woodland in Bolton, Vermont, in 2017 and began restoring its ecosystem.
articles.body: Vermont forester Ethan Tapper bought 175 acres of degraded woodland in Bolton, Vermont, in 2017 and began restoring its ecosystem. The property, which he named Bear Island, had been affected by decades of logging, invasive plant growth and soil erosion. Over the following years, Tapper selectively cut trees, removed invasive vegetation, planted acorns and repaired damage left by earlier land use. He also transformed a rubbish-filled clearing into a pond, where frogs and salamanders appeared within months. The woodland now features a diverse forest understory, habitat for several bird species and an orchard containing more than 100 fruit trees. His work has turned the property into a long-term conservation project focused on improving forest health and habitat diversity.How a Vermont forester spent nine years restoring a damaged forestWhen Tapper acquired Bear Island, the property reflected its history as pastureland and a woodlot. Earlier logging had removed many healthy trees, leaving behind diseased and poorly formed growth. Eroded logging roads crossed the land, while a clearing once used for timber storage was littered with rubbish.Tapper began by selectively removing trees to give healthier specimens more room to grow. He also cleared diseased beech trees, stabilised eroding trails and planted tens of thousands of acorns to encourage future forest growth.His approach combines tree management with efforts to improve the woodland's overall structure. A 2025 profile by forestry equipment manufacturer Tigercat described around 30 acres of regenerating forest with a diverse understory among the results of his work.He turned a rubbish-filled clearing into a pondOne of the most visible changes at Bear Island involved a clearing previously used to store timber. Tapper and a friend rented an excavator and dug a pond, replacing a rubbish-filled area with a water feature.The pond is approximately 20 feet deep and about half the length of a football field. According to Audubon, frogs and salamanders appeared within months of its creation, adding amphibians to the wildlife associated with the recovering property.Rich vegetation and an orchard of more than 100 fruit treesThe woodland now supports a varied understory, including bracken and several fern species. These plants grow beneath the main forest canopy, contributing to the diversity of vegetation across the property.Tapper has also established an orchard containing more than 100 fruit trees. Alongside the pond and regenerating woodland, the orchard adds another distinct feature to the landscape.Birds recorded on the property include American redstarts, veeries, black-throated blue warblers and mourning warblers, according to Audubon. In 2023, Tapper became one of Audubon's first endorsed foresters in Vermont. The programme promotes forest-management practices designed to support birds and other wildlife.A conservation easement protects the propertyIn 2022, Tapper donated a conservation easement on Bear Island, placing permanent legal protections on the land. Such agreements restrict certain uses of a property to preserve its conservation value.The easement extends the project's long-term impact by helping safeguard the woodland beyond Tapper's ownership. It complements the practical work carried out on the property by providing a legal framework for its continued protection.How Ethan Tapper shared his experienceTapper documented his work in his 2024 book, How to Love a Forest: The Bittersweet Work of Tending a Changing World. Drawing on his experience at Bear Island, the book explores forest ecology and the decisions involved in managing woodland.Through articles, talks and social media, Tapper also explains how forestry practices can influence ecosystem health. His work highlights the role of selective cutting, invasive-species management and habitat improvement in caring for forests affected by earlier land use.Nearly nine years after purchasing Bear Island, Tapper continues to manage the woodland and its orchard. The pond, diverse vegetation and regenerating forest reflect the results of sustained work on a landscape once heavily altered by logging and other human activities.You use AI every day. articles.title: In the early 1960s, a Texas oilman started Y Bar O Ranch with 3,520 acres; six decades later, the family’s 29,071-acre Big Bend property sold after being listed for $46.5 million
articles.summary: In the early 1960s, Midland oilman W.B. “Dub” Yarborough and his wife, Kay, began building the Y Bar O Ranch with a 3,520-acre tract in West Texas.
articles.body: In the early 1960s, Midland oilman W.B. “Dub” Yarborough and his wife, Kay, began building the Y Bar O Ranch with a 3,520-acre tract in West Texas. Over the following decades, the family expanded it into a 29,071-acre cattle and recreational property in the Big Bend region. The ranch was listed for $46.5 million on December 9, 2025, and sold on April 14, 2026, according to The Land Report. Although DTN Progressive Farmer reported the transaction as a $46.5 million sale, the final closing price has not been independently established by the available reporting. The ranch is located about 17 miles south of Alpine along Highway 118. Its pastures, livestock facilities, water infrastructure and varied terrain were among the features highlighted in the sale coverage. The transaction ended roughly six decades of ownership by the Yarborough family.Y Bar O Ranch history: how a 3,520-acre tract expanded across West TexasThe Y Bar O Ranch was established in the early 1960s by W.B. “Dub” Yarborough and his wife, Kay, according to DTN Progressive Farmer. Yarborough was a Midland oilman, and the original 3,520-acre tract grew through subsequent acquisitions into a property covering 29,071 acres. The expansion included additions in 1962 and 1966, followed by further acquisitions in 2011 and 2012, according to DTN’s report, which cites the Houston Chronicle. The resulting property became a large cattle and recreational operation in Brewster County, in the Big Bend region of West Texas.The ranch lies about 17 miles south of Alpine along Highway 118. Its terrain varies across the property, from rolling grassland and oak-lined draws in the north to rockier ground, mesas and canyons farther south. In an interview with The Land Report, Chad Dugger of Hall and Hall, the broker who handled the listing, described this north-to-south contrast as one of the ranch’s defining characteristics. The Land Report also highlighted Calamity Creek, seasonal springs and water in canyons between the mesas. These features form part of the ranch’s landscape and support its use as a working cattle property.Y Bar O Ranch facilities: 21 pastures, 10 sets of working pens and water infrastructureThe ranch’s infrastructure was a central feature of its listing. According to Hall and Hall, the property includes a custom-built main residence with more than 4,000 square feet of living space, 4 ensuite bedrooms and radiant-heated floors. Other buildings include a manager’s home, bunkhouse, office, shops, barns, a roping area and a secondary camp in the southern part of the property. For livestock operations, the ranch is divided into 21 pastures and has 10 sets of working pens. The Land Report describes it as a cow-calf operation, a system in which cattle are raised with the aim of producing calves.Water access is another important part of the property. The Land Report reports more than two dozen wells and troughs across the ranch, alongside Calamity Creek and seasonal springs. DTN also describes water storage, pipelines and troughs, with wells powered by a combination of solar, wind and electricity. The ranch supports wildlife including elk, mule deer, aoudad, mountain lions, black bears and upland birds, according to The Land Report. DTN also reports that the property includes livestock equipment and seller-owned mineral interests. Dugger told The Land Report that the quality of the ranch’s upkeep was one of its principal strengths. He singled out the condition of the roads and credited ranch manager Cody Wood and his crew with maintaining them. Dugger said the roads made it possible to tour the property comfortably and see its different areas during a full-day visit.Y Bar O Ranch sale: $46.5 million asking price and a transaction in 2026The Y Bar O Ranch went on the market on December 9, 2025, with an asking price of $46.5 million. According to The Land Report, it went under contract within weeks and sold on April 14, 2026, after only a handful of showings. The Land Report said the buyer and financial terms were not disclosed. DTN Progressive Farmer described the transaction as a $46.5 million sale, attributing that information to Hall and Hall. However, the available reports do not independently confirm the final amount paid. Hall and Hall’s listing displayed an asking price of $46,513,600, so that figure should not be presented as a verified closing price without further confirmation.In his interview with The Land Report, Dugger said Texas land values had risen rapidly after the COVID-19 pandemic. He also observed that sellers could no longer price properties substantially above current market levels and expect the same response from buyers. Those remarks reflect the broker’s assessment of the market, rather than a comprehensive measure of prices across Texas. The sale brought an end to roughly six decades of Yarborough family ownership. The ranch’s history shows how an initial 3,520-acre tract expanded through successive acquisitions into a 29,071-acre working property. Its pastures, livestock facilities, water systems and maintained roads were all documented features of the ranch as it entered the market.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Research ships & seabed surveys: Inside China’s grey-zone tactics against Taiwan
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Chinese military aircraft and vessels appearing around Taiwan have become a near-daily reminder for the island's military to remain alert to
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Chinese military aircraft and vessels appearing around Taiwan have become a near-daily reminder for the island's military to remain alert to Beijing's next move. But beyond warships and fighter jets, another category of vessels is drawing growing scrutiny: Chinese research ships that operate in waters around the island under the stated purpose of conducting scientific surveys.A Reuters investigation published on October 8 reported the first known sighting of a Chinese maritime militia fishing boat off Taiwan's Pacific coast, operating alongside a coast guard cutter and a research vessel. The report added to Taipei's longstanding concerns about what it describes as China's "grey-zone harassment", a pattern of activity that falls short of open warfare but can steadily challenge Taiwan's maritime control and exhaust its surveillance resources.The concern is that some ostensibly civilian research operations may also generate information useful to the People's Liberation Army (PLA), including data on seabed topography, underwater conditions and critical infrastructure. Such information can have legitimate scientific applications, but it can also be relevant to submarine operations and undersea warfare planning.The question facing Taiwan is whether Beijing is using scientific research, maritime law enforcement and civilian vessels as part of a broader strategy to increase pressure on the island without triggering an outright military confrontation.What is grey-zone harassment, and why does Taiwan use the term?Grey-zone activity refers to actions that apply pressure on an opponent without crossing the clear threshold of armed conflict. These can include coast guard patrols, surveillance, fishing fleets linked to state agencies, seabed surveys and demands that commercial ships comply with another country's claimed authority.Taiwan argues that China is combining these activities to challenge its control over surrounding waters. Beijing considers Taiwan part of its territory and maintains that its activities are lawful. Taipei rejects China's sovereignty claims.In his August 18, 2026, report, Science as Statecraft: Chinese Research Vessel Operations Around Taiwan, Allen Zhang of The Heritage Foundation argues that Chinese research ships could help Beijing gather maritime intelligence while giving its operations a civilian appearance.The report identifies four potential strategic uses:Seabed mapping: Collecting information about underwater terrain and ocean conditions that can affect submarine operations.Undersea cable intelligence: Identifying the location and vulnerability of cables carrying internet and communications traffic.Surveillance: Observing military exercises and the movements of Taiwanese or allied forces.Maritime claims: Repeatedly operating in contested waters to create an impression that China exercises authority there.These are potential uses and strategic assessments. A vessel's presence in an area does not, by itself, prove that it is conducting military intelligence operations.Why research vessels matter to military plannersResearch ships can carry sonar equipment, seabed-mapping systems, oceanographic sensors, remotely operated vehicles and other instruments. These technologies have legitimate scientific uses, but the resulting data can also be useful to naval forces.Water temperature, salinity, currents and seabed topography influence how sound travels underwater. This affects the detection of submarines and the performance of sonar systems. Detailed environmental data can therefore help navies assess where submarines may operate or be detected.Seabed surveys can also reveal terrain around submarine cables and other underwater infrastructure. Such information can be relevant to infrastructure protection, repair planning and military contingency planning.A research vessel positioned near a military exercise may be able to observe vessel movements and collect environmental or other data. Whether a particular ship has done so requires evidence beyond its location alone.The Heritage Foundation says China's Ministry of Natural Resources (MNR) operates the largest share of the country's maritime research fleet, which it describes as the world's largest. The report examines institutional links between civilian maritime research and China's military establishment, including research vessels that were previously registered with the People's Liberation Army Navy (PLAN).These links are relevant to China's broader military-civil fusion strategy, which seeks to integrate civilian research, technology and industrial capacity with national defence. They do not establish that every research voyage has a military purpose.Date-wise timeline: Chinese maritime activity around Taiwan2024: Xiang Yang Hong 06 and seabed-mapping concernsThe Heritage Foundation says the Chinese research vessel Xiang Yang Hong 06 was observed moving slowly in precise lines along Taiwan's east coast. Naval experts cited by the paper considered the pattern consistent with seabed mapping.Such movement can be consistent with systematic surveying, although it does not independently establish the ship's precise mission.May 7, 2026: Taiwan challenges the TongjiTaiwan's coast guard said it detected the Chinese research vessel Tongji about 29 nautical miles southeast of Taiwan's southern tip. The ship was seen lowering ropes into the water, which Taiwanese authorities suspected were connected to survey instruments.A Taiwanese coast guard vessel moved close to the ship and broadcast warnings. Taiwan said Tongji retrieved its equipment and changed course.Reuters published its report on May 11. China did not immediately respond to a request for comment.June 6-10, 2026: Chinese agencies conduct a maritime enforcement operationThe International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) reported a joint Chinese operation involving the China Coast Guard, Maritime Safety Administration and transport ministry's Rescue and Salvage Bureau.According to IISS, Chinese vessels hailed commercial ships, remotely inspected 198 vessels and questioned three about their ports of departure and arrival and the number of crew aboard. The three vessels were flagged in Benin, Liberia and Singapore.Taiwan said the operation sought to create a false impression of Chinese jurisdiction over waters east of the island.June 16, 2026: Xiang Yang Hong 22 conducts a marine surveyThe Heritage Foundation says the research vessel Xiang Yang Hong 22, operating under China's East China Sea Bureau, conducted a survey east of Taiwan. The stated purpose was to understand ecological conditions and support marine conservation.The report places this activity within the broader increase in Chinese research operations around the island.June-July 2026: Coast guard patrols expand east of TaiwanIISS reported Chinese coast guard patrols east of Taiwan in June, followed by further patrols in July, August and September.The broader concern is that Beijing is relying on a range of state agencies rather than exclusively on the navy. Civilian and law-enforcement vessels can maintain a presence without sending the same immediate military signal as a large naval deployment.July 17-23, 2026: Lanhai 201's survey raises questionsThe Chinese research vessel Lanhai 201, operated by the East China Sea Fisheries Research Institute, conducted a survey east of Taiwan. Chinese authorities described it as fisheries-resource research.On July 23, Taiwan's coast guard said the vessel was 53 nautical miles east-northeast of Lanyu, also known as Orchid Island, travelling north at 13.5 knots. Taiwan said its patrol vessel continued monitoring the ship.The Heritage Foundation later pointed to unusual speed and course changes in publicly available tracking data as grounds for questioning whether the voyage was limited to fisheries research. That is an assessment of the vessel's behaviour, not proof of a covert military mission.August 10-31, 2026: China conducts a seabed survey east of TaiwanChina's Ministry of Natural Resources conducted a survey intended to examine the geology and structural characteristics of the seabed, according to Chinese state broadcaster CCTV in a report cited by Reuters on September 3.Taiwan's coast guard monitored the operation and rejected Beijing's claim to jurisdiction over the surrounding waters. China presented the survey as part of resource management and territorial planning.Mid-August 2026: Three-vessel group spotted off Taiwan's east coastA surveillance report by Taiwan's Apex Aviation, reviewed by Reuters, identified three vessels operating within roughly a 10-nautical-mile radius more than 30 nautical miles off Hualien.The vessels were:Minfudingyu 07902, identified as a Chinese fishing boat that doubles as a maritime militia vessel.China Coast Guard cutter 2502.Research vessel Xiang Yang Hong 03.Two Taiwanese officials confirmed the vessels' presence. They said the fishing boat was part of China's maritime militia and was operating in coordination with coast guard activity.The surveillance did not establish the exact mission of each vessel or conclusively prove coordination among all three.September 3, 2026: Beijing acknowledges the August surveyReuters reported China's announcement that its Ministry of Natural Resources had surveyed waters east of Taiwan from August 10 to 31. China said the work would support a unified map for territorial planning and resource management.China's coast guard also announced a routine patrol east of Taiwan on September 3, described by Reuters as the third such patrol since June.October 8, 2026: Reuters reports the militia boat sightingReuters published its investigation into the August sighting of the suspected Chinese maritime militia fishing boat off Taiwan's east coast.Taiwan's defence ministry said China was using law enforcement and scientific research as cover for harassment and to create an illusion of de facto jurisdiction. China's Taiwan Affairs Office and defence ministry did not respond to Reuters' requests for comment.The report brought renewed attention to the overlap between Chinese research vessels, coast guard ships and suspected maritime militia craft.Why Taiwan's east coast mattersTaiwan's east coast faces the Pacific and is important to its ability to receive supplies and support from partners during a crisis. The western side of the island faces mainland China across the Taiwan Strait, while its eastern maritime approaches offer access to the wider Pacific.The Heritage Foundation identifies three underwater regions around Taiwan where Chinese research vessels have been observed since June 2026:Okinawa Trough, north of Taiwan: An underwater region between Taiwan and the Ryukyu island chain.Huatung Basin, east of Taiwan: An area relevant to understanding the seabed and ocean conditions off Taiwan's Pacific coast.Luzon Trough and Manila Trench, south of Taiwan: Underwater features near routes linking the South China Sea and the western Pacific.The report says the vessels had not surveyed the Taiwan Strait during the period it examined. Their activity instead covered areas north, east and south of the island.The wider geographic spread is part of the concern. Surveys of the approaches around Taiwan could provide information relevant to monitoring and operating in the waters surrounding the island.What coral reefs and artificial islands have to do with China's maritime strategyCoral reefs and seabed surveys are related to the wider picture of China's maritime ambitions, but they should not be confused with the specific research-vessel incidents east of Taiwan.In the South China Sea, China has used dredging and land reclamation to expand its presence on disputed reefs. These projects can create space for runways, ports, radar systems and other infrastructure. A reef that was previously difficult to occupy can become a fixed base for maritime surveillance and military operations.A Reuters investigation published on October 2, 2026, reported that construction of a runway on Antelope Reef in the Paracel Islands was well underway. Satellite imagery dated September 25 showed ground preparation, gravel piles, compaction equipment and a gravel barge heading towards a newly built wharf.Analysts cited by Reuters estimated that the runway could be completed by mid-2027. China has not acknowledged that it is building a new military base there. Chinese state media have described Antelope as serving civilian purposes, including weather forecasting, maritime services and scientific research.The Paracel Islands are also claimed by Vietnam and Taiwan. China has occupied the islands since driving out forces of then-South Vietnam in a 1974 battle.The relevance to Taiwan is strategic rather than geographical. Antelope Reef is in the South China Sea, not off Taiwan's east coast. The project illustrates how infrastructure initially described in civilian or scientific terms can also improve a state's ability to monitor and operate across contested maritime areas.For Taiwan, the concern is that surveys, patrols and fixed infrastructure could reinforce one another: research ships collect data, coast guard vessels maintain a presence, and bases elsewhere in the region support longer deployments.Undersea cables: A potential vulnerability in a Taiwan crisisTaiwan depends on undersea fibre-optic cables for international internet and communications links. These cables are difficult to monitor continuously and can be damaged by accidents, fishing activity or deliberate interference.The Heritage Foundation's report argues that research vessels could help identify cable routes and surrounding seabed conditions. It also cites two cable outages affecting Taiwan's Matsu Islands in February 2023, when Taiwan accused China of severing the links. Those accusations should not be treated as proof that the cables were deliberately cut by China.The paper also points to a deep-sea cable-cutting device unveiled by a Chinese research institute in 2025, which Chinese scientists said was intended for marine resource development. The report says the device was designed to operate at depths of up to 4,000 metres.The strategic concern is that damage to multiple cables during a crisis could disrupt communications and complicate coordination with external partners. However, the existence of a capability does not establish that it has been deployed against Taiwan.The blockade scenario: How grey-zone activity could help BeijingTaiwanese officials are concerned that China could use repeated patrols and inspections to prepare for a potential maritime blockade or quarantine.A blockade would involve restricting access to Taiwan's ports and sea routes. A quarantine could instead be presented as a law-enforcement operation, with Chinese authorities demanding that commercial vessels provide information, submit to inspections or comply with Chinese instructions.The distinction matters because a law-enforcement operation may be more difficult to treat as an immediate military attack than a naval blockade. It could also force Taiwan and its partners to decide how to respond to individual incidents without escalating into armed conflict.The Heritage Foundation identifies three ways the current activity could contribute to such a scenario:Operational familiarity: Repeated deployments can improve knowledge of sea routes, vessel movements and operating conditions.Administrative pressure: Demands for shipping information can test whether Beijing can make commercial operators comply with its claims.Normalisation: Regular patrols may gradually make a Chinese presence appear routine, even where Taiwan disputes China's authority.These are potential strategic benefits identified by the report, not evidence that Beijing has decided to impose a blockade.Why Taiwan cannot simply drive every vessel awayResearch vessels are not necessarily warships. They may be conducting legitimate scientific work, and their presence outside restricted waters does not automatically establish an unlawful act.That creates a difficult response problem for Taiwan. Forcefully expelling a civilian vessel could give Beijing grounds to accuse Taipei of obstructing legitimate research. Allowing repeated operations to continue without a response could, in Taiwan's view, encourage further activity.Taiwan has responded through coast guard patrols, warnings, surveillance and the monitoring of vessel movements. The Apex Aviation operation also shows how civilian surveillance capabilities can contribute to maritime awareness. Its aircraft used radar, infrared imagery and automatic identification system data to document the August vessel group.The United States has also expressed concern about Chinese activity east of Taiwan. On October 10, the US State Department described the activity as “deeply destabilising” and urged Beijing to stop pressuring Taiwan and engage in dialogue with its democratically elected authorities.What the evidence establishes, and what remains uncertainThe reported incidents establish that Chinese research vessels and other state-linked maritime actors have been operating around Taiwan, including in areas east of the island. Taiwan has monitored or challenged some of these operations, while China has publicly described at least some surveys as scientific or resource-management work.The evidence does not establish that every research vessel is conducting military surveillance, that the three vessels seen off Hualien were carrying out a confirmed joint mission, or that China is preparing to launch a blockade imminently.The stronger conclusion is that Beijing's maritime presence is becoming more varied, combining research activity, coast guard operations and suspected maritime militia deployments. That combination could provide China with information, persistence and political leverage while making it harder for Taiwan to determine which activities require a stronger response.The next indicators to watch are whether Chinese research ships return to the same underwater regions, whether coast guard patrols become more regular, whether commercial ships face more demands for information, and whether new surveillance or infrastructure activity appears along Taiwan's eastern approaches..You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2001, Pierre Cardin bought the ruined château once owned by the Marquis de Sade; after nearly seven years and millions of euros in restoration work, the historic Provence site became a music and theatre festival venue
articles.summary: High above the Luberon Valley in southern France, an old hilltop castle once linked to the infamous Marquis de Sade has been given a new purpose after
articles.body: High above the Luberon Valley in southern France, an old hilltop castle once linked to the infamous Marquis de Sade has been given a new purpose after years of restoration. French fashion designer Pierre Cardin bought the 11th-century Château de Lacoste in 2001 to save it from further damage. He spent millions of euros on repairs and restoration work. Nearly seven years after the project began, the site reopened as a venue for an annual international music and theatre festival. The castle, once known for its links to 18th-century scandal, became an active centre for the performing arts.Origins and aristocratic scandalThe history of Château de Lacoste dates back to the 11th century, when it served as a fortified stronghold for the Simiane family. According to historical records published in the France-Voyage regional archive, the property passed to the Sade family, a powerful family from Provence, in the early 18th century. In 1763, Donatien Alphonse François de Sade, later known as the Marquis de Sade, inherited the estate. The writer and aristocrat used the castle as a retreat when he escaped legal authorities in Paris. Away from the city, he organised private theatrical performances in an auditorium built for that purpose. The estate suffered serious damage during the French Revolution. In 1792, local uprisings led to widespread looting and the partial destruction of the castle walls. Much of the original stone was later sold and reused as building material. The ruins remained in private hands but received little attention for generations. In 1952, college professor André Bouer bought the site and began work to make the remaining structure more stable. This effort continued for nearly five decades. In 1992, the French Ministry of Culture officially listed the castle, its courtyards and its dry moats as a historic monument.Cardin's multi-million euro acquisition and restorationIn January 2001, fashion designer Pierre Cardin bought the ruined estate. His aim was to prevent the historic structure from collapsing and turn the property into a place for artistic activities. Over the next seven years, Cardin invested millions of euros in major repairs and conservation work. Workers strengthened the surviving medieval walls, removed centuries of debris from the nearby stone quarries and repaired interior rooms so they could be used for public visits and exhibitions. The damage to the castle had caused deep distress to its former owner. "I am in despair! It is above expression," the Marquis de Sade wrote in 1792 after the initial destruction of his residence, according to historical correspondence cited by the regional heritage archive Comme des Français. Cardin wanted to give the site a different future. He developed a modern cultural centre next to the ancient ruins and turned the surrounding stone quarries into an open-air amphitheatre. The venue was designed to host large opera productions, concerts and theatrical performances.The birth of the Lacoste FestivalBy the late 2000s, the former military stronghold had become the permanent home of the Festival de Lacoste. The annual summer event features opera, dance and classical theatre. According to the official Festival de Lacoste programme, the open-air venue benefits from the natural acoustics created by the surrounding hillside quarry walls. The location also offers views across the Calavon Valley towards Mont Ventoux and the neighbouring village of Bonnieux. "In the heart of the Luberon, the luminous beauty of Lacoste welcomes each year the Festival of Opera and Theater, in this unique place so dear to the Marquis de Sade," Cardin stated in event documentation published by Agence Rosier. The festival is not the only attraction at the estate. The castle's interior courtyards and restored upper rooms were also opened to visitors. These areas display Cardin's personal art collection, period furniture and theatrical costumes, giving visitors a closer look at the site's history and its connection to the arts.Impact on the village of LacosteCardin's purchase of the castle was part of a wider property investment project in the village of Lacoste. According to records compiled in the French national encyclopedia, Cardin bought more than 40 separate properties, shops and old houses along the narrow cobbled streets below the castle walls. His investments brought fresh commercial activity to the village, although they also raised concerns among some residents about property ownership and the protection of historic buildings in small rural communities. The debate over commercial development has continued alongside efforts to preserve the area's history. Despite these concerns, Château de Lacoste remains one of the main historical and cultural landmarks in the Vaucluse department. Today, the castle serves two purposes. It stands as a protected example of France's 18th-century history while also providing a venue for live performances during the summer. Cardin's restoration helped preserve the remaining medieval structure and gave the once-neglected estate a continuing role in the cultural life of the Luberon region.You use AI every day. articles.title: In Queensland, Steve Irwin and his wife Terri turned an avocado shed into a wildlife rescue hospital in 2004; more than 136,000 animals were treated over the following two decades
articles.summary: An avocado packing shed might seem an unlikely place to begin a major wildlife rescue operation, but that was where Steve and Terri Irwin started their
articles.body: An avocado packing shed might seem an unlikely place to begin a major wildlife rescue operation, but that was where Steve and Terri Irwin started their hospital in Queensland in 2004. The project grew from a long-standing concern for injured and orphaned animals, inspired in part by Steve’s mother, Lyn Irwin, and her work in wildlife rehabilitation. According to Wildlife Warriors, two decades later, the Australia Zoo Wildlife Hospital had treated more than 136,000 animals, marking a considerable change in scale from its modest beginnings. Today, the facility provides specialist veterinary care for thousands of native Australian animals each year.How Steve and Terri Irwin turned an avocado shed into a wildlife hospitalThe hospital's early history is closely linked to Lyn Irwin, Steve Irwin's mother, who cared for wildlife and rehabilitated injured animals. Her ambition to establish a dedicated treatment facility helped shape the project that Steve and Terri went on to develop.In 2004, the couple transformed an existing avocado packing shed into a working hospital. The initial facility offered a practical response to the need for somewhere to treat wild animals that could not be cared for adequately in ordinary veterinary settings. It also gave the zoo a dedicated base for handling injured wildlife brought in from the surrounding area.The Wildlife Warriors reported the operation expanded as more animals required assistance. On 15 November 2008, which is observed as Steve Irwin Day, a new hospital building opened to accommodate the growing number of patients. The move marked a significant change from the converted shed, providing a purpose-built setting for wildlife medicine.More than 136,000 animals treated at Australia Zoo wildlife hospitalBy 2024, more than 136,000 animals had passed through the hospital since its early years. The cumulative figure offers a measure of the work carried out since the facility was established, covering animals brought in for a range of injuries and other problems.The hospital continues to receive thousands of patients each year. Wildlife Warriors, the conservation organisation associated with the Irwin family, says between 9,000 and 10,000 animals are admitted over a 12-month period. Patients include native mammals, birds and reptiles, with treatment needs ranging from injuries caused by road traffic to cases involving orphaned young or ingestion of foreign material.How Australia Zoo provides specialist care for injured native wildlifeThe hospital has facilities including a surgical theatre, an X-ray room, intensive care units and a pathology laboratory. Its veterinary team includes wildlife veterinarians and nurses who assess patients and provide treatment suited to different species and injuries.A kangaroo struck by a vehicle may need surgery or rehabilitation, while a young koala without its mother may require specialised care before it can move into the next stage of recovery. Sea turtles brought in after swallowing plastic present a different set of challenges.According to Wildlife Warriors, treatment is provided without charge to the public, and native wildlife is not refused care because of the cost of its treatment. Running the facility nevertheless involves considerable expense, from staffing and medical supplies to maintaining specialist equipment and intensive care spaces.From Steve Irwin’s conservation mission to a major wildlife hospitalSteve Irwin became internationally known for his wildlife television programmes and hands-on approach to conservation. The hospital represents a different part of that work, concentrating on animals that need direct medical attention rather than public education alone.The project also reflects the influence of his mother, whose interest in wildlife rehabilitation helped inspire the facility. What began in a converted agricultural building developed into a larger hospital as the number of patients increased and the need for dedicated facilities became clearer.The Irwin family's conservation work continues through Australia Zoo and Wildlife Warriors, with the hospital providing treatment for native animals brought in by members of the public and others involved in wildlife rescue.You use AI every day. articles.title: Parents go ballistic at California school after four blonde girls shared blackface picture — as other shocking incidents emerge
articles.summary: Santa Barbara parents are aghast at the appearance of willful ignorance from a local school district after four teenage girls posted a TikTok in blackface la...
articles.body:
California parents are furious at a school district after four teenage girls posted a TikTok in blackface last month.

The girls were disciplined, but parents claimed their conduct is part of a pattern at Santa Barbara Unified School District.

Parents sat with signs decrying racism at a school board meeting on Tuesday night. Signs read things like, "Don't be a bystander, stop ignoring racism," and "What was the reason it took two weeks and some to notify parents?" and "racism doesn't disappear when it's swept under the rug."

Most of the signs were made because of an organized protest in favor of black students and demanded action from the district.

Most of the discourse surrounded the girls' TikTok video in which the girls are seen mimicking an AI-generated image of four young black boys in various poses. "Meet the gc

…," the post is captioned. The ninja emoji is known to be used as a reference to the N-word.

San Marcos High School Principal Dare Holdren previously said the students "portrayed blackface" in the post and noted the school "instituted consequences" for the girls.

Parents wondered why it took Holdren two weeks to notify them of the incident.

"Parents deserve to know," Leticia Forney Resch, an executive director for Healing Justice Santa Barbara, said. "They had pictures and images going out to students for a week-and-a-half… Y'all didn't do your job."

The girls posed for the picture in an African American studies classroom. The teacher who uses the room as his classroom expressed outrage at the racism in the school.

"When black students are harmed, every student is harmed," Abel Gonzalez, the ethnic studies teacher at San Marcos High School, said. "Black and brown students are very upset and trying to heal."

Other racist incidents have rattled the school district in the past.

According to the Santa Barbara Independent , a San Marcos High School substitute teacher read the N-word out loud during a reading of "Of Mice and Men" last year after being told not to. The substitute was then removed from campus.

A parent said the district has just watched racism escalate.

"When a nation refuses to confront institutional and structural racism, the harm does not stay contained, it escalates," Charlotte Gullap-Moore said. "Santa Barbara Unified has watched that escalation in its own schools."

The local NAACP previously criticized the school for failing to establish protocols to respond to incidents of racism.

"SBUSD has struggled to establish protocols to respond to racial incidents and execute them with humanity. Principals need clear guidance; parents and students need accessible information about district investigations and potential disciplinary actions for racist incidents ," NAACP Santa Barbara President Connie Alexander wrote in an op-ed for the Santa Barbara Independent.

Even teachers say the only way the school district can remedy the situation is action.

"Doing nothing tells this community that anti-Black bias and racism is woven into the fabric of Santa Barbara schools," Moore, speaking on behalf of Santa Barbara Unified teacher Tahnia Mark, said. "So be honest, do you really care about black students? If you don't, just say it…Otherwise, show through action."

articles.title: Rahul & Priyanka meet Ankita Bhandari's parents at India Gate; all about 2022 Uttarakhand murder case
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Leader of opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi and Congress MP Priyanka Gandhi Vadra arrived at India Gate in New Delhi on Wednesday to
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Leader of opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi and Congress MP Priyanka Gandhi Vadra arrived at India Gate in New Delhi on Wednesday to meet the parents of Ankita Bhandari, who was murdered in Uttarakhand in 2022.Ankita’s parents staged a protest near India Gate, demanding that the appointment of BJP leader Dushyant Kumar Gautam as Sikkim Governor be put on hold until the ongoing Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) probe into the case is completed.Rahul had previously met Bhandari's parents in August and mentioned that four years have passed, yet they are still awaiting justice for the unforgivable crime committed against their daughter.Ankita’s father, Virendra Singh Bhandari, urged President Droupadi Murmu not to appoint Gautam as Governor until the investigation concludes.“Dushyant Kumar should be behind bars... I earnestly request the Honorable President not to appoint Dushyant Kumar as Governor until the CBI investigation is concluded,” he said, according to news agency ANI.Ankita’s mother, Soni Devi, also appealed to the President to halt the appointment.“We were deeply pained when we heard the news on the 12th that he (BJP leader Dushyant Kumar Gautam) has now been named Governor. I appeal to the Honorable President, who is herself a woman and will surely understand my sentiments, to halt the move to appoint this individual as Governor until the CBI investigation against him is concluded,” she said.What is the Ankita Bhandari murder case?Ankita, 19, worked as a receptionist at the Vanantra Resort in Rishikesh. She was killed on September 18, 2022, and her body was recovered from the Chilla canal four days later.Resort owner Pulkit Arya, the son of former BJP leader Vinod Arya, and two accomplices were convicted in the case and sentenced to life imprisonment.The case also drew political attention over allegations that an unidentified VIP was linked to the crime.Ankita’s family and activists have repeatedly demanded an investigation into this alleged VIP angle, with Gautam’s name being raised in connection with the allegations.The allegations against Gautam remain unproven. He has denied them and initiated defamation proceedings against those making the accusations.Why are Ankita’s parents opposing Gautam’s appointment?Gautam was appointed Sikkim Governor on Monday. Ankita’s parents have demanded that the appointment be put on hold until the CBI investigation is complete.Her father alleged that a VIP had played a major role in his daughter’s murder and claimed that Gautam was responsible. He questioned the decision to appoint Gautam as Governor while the investigation was ongoing.“We have heard that the VIP had a major role in my daughter’s murder. Now, the Centre and the Uttarakhand government have appointed Gautam as the governor of Sikkim,” he said.“We humbly request the government and the President of India that he should not be appointed Sikkim governor until the CBI investigation into the case is over,” he added.Her mother, Soni Devi, also urged that the appointment be stopped until the probe concludes.The parents said they had sought an appointment with President Droupadi Murmu to raise their concerns. They warned that if their demand was not met, they would sit on a hunger strike outside the Uttarakhand chief minister’s Office at the Secretariat in Dehradun.Political row over the appointmentThe appointment has also drawn opposition from the Uttarakhand Congress, which has alleged that Gautam’s name surfaced in connection with the murder case.The Congress has claimed that the appointment was intended to shield Gautam, arguing that a Governor cannot be subjected to criminal proceedings while holding office.Gautam, a former national general secretary of the BJP, had served as the party’s in-charge for Uttarakhand.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2020, Selena Gomez launched the Rare Impact Fund alongside Rare Beauty; six years later it has raised over $30 million, supports 30 nonprofits and reaches about 3.5 million young people each year
articles.summary: When Selena Gomez launched Rare Beauty in 2020, she also created the Rare Impact Fund, a philanthropic initiative dedicated to expanding access to youth
articles.body: When Selena Gomez launched Rare Beauty in 2020, she also created the Rare Impact Fund, a philanthropic initiative dedicated to expanding access to youth mental health services. Six years later, the fund has raised more than $30 million, supports 30 nonprofit partners across five continents, and reaches about 3.5 million young people annually. According to PR Newswire, the fund’s long-term goal is to mobilise $100 million for organisations that increase access to mental health services and education worldwide.The numbers reflect more than fundraising success. They show how a beauty brand can be built around a social mission from the beginning, with part of every sale directed toward a cause that Gomez has spoken about openly. The Rare Impact Fund has grown into a global network of partners, donors, and young people seeking support. Read more details about it here:Why Gomez started the fundGomez has been candid about her own mental health journey, and the Rare Impact Fund was created as part of her broader focus on addressing mental health. The initiative supports organisations that help young people access care, education, and resources when they need them.Mental health support is often unevenly distributed, particularly for young people who may not know where to seek help or cannot afford professional services. The fund aims to reduce those barriers by backing nonprofits that provide direct services and expand mental health education.Gomez has said that shining a light on youth mental health is not something that can be done alone. Her comments ahead of the fund’s fourth annual benefit emphasised the importance of sponsors, artists, and supporters in reaching millions of young people around the world.How the fund raises moneyOne percent of all Rare Beauty sales is donated to the Rare Impact Fund, as per the report. That ongoing contribution means the brand’s customers participate in the mission through their purchases, rather than the fund depending only on large one-time donations. The fund also raises additional money through philanthropic foundations, individual donors, corporate partners, and the Rare Beauty community. It operates as a fiscally sponsored project of the Hopewell Fund, a 501(c)(3) public charity.This structure has helped the initiative grow beyond its original launch. Since 2020, it has raised more than $30 million and built partnerships with 30 nonprofits working across five continents.A global reachThe Rare Impact Fund now reaches about 3.5 million young people each year. Its support extends to organisations working to increase access to mental health services and education for young people worldwide.The fund’s nonprofit partners operate across five continents, reflecting an understanding that mental health needs vary across communities and cultures. Rather than treating the issue as a single problem with one solution, the fund supports local organisations that understand the needs of the young people they serve.That approach also allows the fund to connect global fundraising with community-level work. Money raised through Rare Beauty sales, donors, and benefit events can help organisations provide counselling, education, crisis support, and other services where they are needed most.The fourth annual benefitThe Rare Impact Fund’s fourth annual Benefit, titled “A Night of Radiance & Reflection,” took place on October 14, 2026, at The Hollywood Palladium in Los Angeles. Gomez hosted the event, while Emmy and Tony Award-winning actor and comedian Sean Hayes served as emcee.Singer Leon Bridges and singer-songwriter Bella Kay performed at the benefit. Bridges said mental health advocacy was crucial and described the opportunity to help create tangible access to support for young people as a privilege.Kay said music had helped her make sense of her own mental health and vulnerabilities. She described the benefit as an evening dedicated to expanding youth mental health support, a cause she said was close to home.Support from brands and advocatesThe 2026 benefit brought together a host committee of leaders, advocates, and supporters of the fund. It included Pacsun CEO Brieane Olson, UCLA Hospital System CEO Johnese Spisso, lululemon’s head of social impact Anne Wintroub, singer Becky G, producer benny blanco, author and host Jay Shetty, and others.Rare level sponsors for the event included Rare Beauty, Afterpay, Batch & Box, lululemon, Pacsun, UCLA Health, and Ulta Beauty. Their support helped fund the benefit and amplify the fund’s mission.The involvement of beauty, retail, health, and entertainment brands shows how youth mental health has become a shared priority across industries. It also gives the fund access to wider audiences than it might reach through philanthropy alone.Momentum from previous eventsThe 2025 benefit raised more than $2 million from more than 20 sponsors and guests. It was hosted by Jimmy Kimmel and featured performances from alternative pop band The Marías and Grammy-winning singer Laufey.Those events have become an important part of the fund’s annual fundraising calendar. They bring together celebrities, corporate sponsors, donors, and advocates while keeping attention focused on the practical need for youth mental health services.The fourth annual benefit continued that momentum. With Leon Bridges and Bella Kay performing, the event aimed to raise further support for organisations working to make mental health care and education more accessible.Why the mission mattersYouth mental health has become one of the most urgent public health issues of the past decade. Young people face pressures related to school, social media, family instability, identity, economic uncertainty, and access to care, and many struggle to find timely support.The Rare Impact Fund’s work matters because it focuses on both services and education. Helping young people access professional support is essential, but teaching them to understand and talk about mental health can also reduce stigma and encourage earlier help-seeking.Gomez’s initiative shows how a personal commitment can become a large-scale platform for change. What began alongside a beauty brand in 2020 has grown into a $30 million effort that reaches millions of young people each year.Looking toward $100 millionThe fund’s stated ambition is to mobilise $100 million for youth mental health organisations around the world. With more than $30 million raised since launch, it has made substantial progress toward that target.The next stage will depend on continued support from Rare Beauty customers, corporate partners, philanthropists, and the wider public. The fund’s benefit events, sponsorships, and global nonprofit network are likely to remain central to that effort.For Gomez, the Rare Impact Fund is more than a corporate social responsibility programme. It is a way to use her platform to make mental health support more visible, more accessible, and less isolating for young people around the world.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: In 2007, a New Yorker paid $3 for a white bowl at a yard sale and kept it in the living room for years; experts later identified it as a 1,000-year-old Chinese artefact, and it sold for $2.225 million
articles.summary: Every New Yorker has walked past a yard sale and kept walking. Most of the time, they’re right to.
articles.body: Every New Yorker has walked past a yard sale and kept walking. Most of the time, they’re right to. The folding tables are full of chipped mugs, mismatched lamps and vases nobody has ever wanted. Every so often, though, one of those tables hides something that makes an auction house very happy and a family very confused.That was the case for one New Yorker who spotted a small white bowl at a yard sale in 2007. Priced at just $3, it looked unique. The buyer thought it was a bargain and took it home. The bowl sat in the buyer’s living room for several years, quietly becoming part of the household. Years later, the owner had it appraised, and experts estimated its value at up to $300,000. The reason? It was a rare Chinese artefact dating back around 1,000 years!An unassuming bowl at the yard saleYard sales are often filled with chipped mugs, discarded furniture and strange decor items, so it is easy to see why a pale bowl would not stand out. This white bowl with a carved design sat there. Its ivory glaze pooled into darker streaks near the base, and rows of moulded leaves wrapped around the outside. Inside, a lotus pattern was carved into the clay. Nothing about it looked like a museum object, which may be the most important detail in the whole story.The bowl’s unique design and intricate workmanship sparked the buyer’s curiosity. They wanted to know what they had. The family kept the bowl in their living room for a few years before deciding to have it appraised, according to Sotheby’s spokeswoman Cecilia Leung.Experts identified the bowl as ‘Ding’ ware, a type of Chinese porcelain made during the Northern Song dynasty, which ruled from 960 to 1127. It was worth between $200,000 and $300,000. Few people expect to hear numbers like that about something they bought for pocket change.A rare Chinese artefactThe bowl was a rare and important example of ‘Ding’ ware. Ding ware was prized for its thin walls and fine white body. This type of porcelain was made in the kiln region of Quyang, in Hebei province, and early pieces were usually plain. Later potters began carving and moulding their designs, and some Ding wares imitated gold and silver vessels, which were far more expensive. ‘The high quality of the potting seen here is evident in the feather-light weight of the bowl, with the carved walls especially thin and delicate,’ the auction house says. The auctioneers described it as ‘rare and exceptionally beautiful’.Collectors of later dynasties grouped Ding ware among the ‘five great wares’ of the Song period, and it is easy to see why. The glaze runs in darker tears near the foot, and the walls are so thin that light can pass through them. Those qualities are hard to fake and harder to find in good condition.The shape of the bowl is also worth noting, as similar designs appear in silver bowls from the Song dynasty. ‘For example, see a bowl illustrated in Zhongguo jin yin poli falangqi quanji, vol. 2 (2), Shijiazhuang, 2000, pl. 261, together with another silver bowl of more rounded body but the exterior moulded with layers of overlapping upright leaves, reminiscent of that seen on this bowl, pl. 262,’ the auction house explained.The rare Ding ware was in ‘good condition’, Sotheby’s said. ‘The rim is very slightly warped, and the foot rim is not perfectly circular. There is a tiny firing tear under the rim on the interior, approx. 1/8 in. (0.4 cm) long; otherwise, the bowl is in overall good condition.’The bowl went up for auction at Sotheby’s in New York in March 2013. Four bidders competed for it, and the price climbed well past the estimate. The winner was Giuseppe Eskenazi, a London-based dealer, who paid $2,225,000. That figure includes the buyer’s commission.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Giant pumpkins become boats in Minnesota’s annual river race, where one competitor honoured her son and another won for the third time
articles.summary: Hundreds of people gathered along the St. Croix River in Stillwater, Minnesota, on Sunday to watch four competitors race in giant, hollowed-out pumpkins.
articles.body: Hundreds of people gathered along the St. Croix River in Stillwater, Minnesota, on Sunday to watch four competitors race in giant, hollowed-out pumpkins. The event, known as the Pumpkin Regatta, took place during the 21st annual Stillwater Harvest Fest in 2026. According to MPR News (Minnesota Public Radio), favourable weather made conditions particularly good for spectators and racers.Tim Brown, a Stillwater native who has competed in the regatta every year for the past decade, won the first-place trophy for the third time. He raced alongside his cousin, Matthew Schmidt, a previous winner of the event. For the first-time racer Laura Fairchild, however, the race was about more than winning. She took part to honour her son, Justin Ross Fairchild, who served in the US Army and died in 2007.St. Croix River hosts four racers in Stillwater's 2026 Pumpkin RegattaThe 2026 Pumpkin Regatta brought four competitors to the St. Croix River, where they paddled giant pumpkins that had been hollowed out before the race. Hundreds of spectators gathered along the river to watch the unusual competition, which is one of only a few events of its kind across the United States.Tim Brown won the first-place trophy for the third time after competing in the regatta every year. He said, “I think the first time I won was in 2016 so to be able to do it in my mid-40s is pretty cool”. He competed alongside his cousin, Matthew Schmidt, a previous winner, and said his biggest goal was to defeat him.Laura Fairchild takes part in the pumpkin race to honour her sonFor first-time racer Laura Fairchild, the Pumpkin Regatta carried a personal meaning beyond the competition. She took part to honour her son, Justin Ross Fairchild, who served in the US Army and died in 2007. Brown acknowledged the difficulty of the task, remarking on the unexpected experience of paddling a pumpkin. articles.title: US proposes ending deference to past H-1B approvals; Indians will be disproportionately impacted
articles.summary: The Trump administration has proposed scrapping a policy that generally requires US immigration officers to defer to their own previous approvals of work
articles.body: The Trump administration has proposed scrapping a policy that generally requires US immigration officers to defer to their own previous approvals of work visa petitions, a move that could make it challenging for Indian professionals to secure H-1B extensions. The proposed policy which also covers other work visas such as L-1 (intra company transfers), is currently open for public comments and could be finalised in a few months.H-1B status is generally granted for an initial period of up to three years, with an extension of up to another three years, taking the usual maximum period of stay in the US to six years. Employers must file extension petitions to retain workers beyond the initial approval period. However, certain workers qualify for extensions beyond the six-year limit, particularly where employment-based green card applications are pending or approved but visa numbers are unavailable – a significant number of Indian professionals qualify for such extensions.The proposed regulation by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) seeks to eliminate the principle of “deference to prior approvals”, under which US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) officers generally rely on earlier decisions when considering subsequent extension applications involving the same parties and underlying facts. “If implemented, the change could lead to greater scrutiny of repeat applications even when a worker’s employment circumstances have not materially changed,” said Mitch Wexler, senior counsel at Fragomen, a global immigration law firm.The implications could be significant for Indian professionals. According to data released earlier this year by USCIS, 2.26 lakh H-1B applications for Indian-born beneficiaries were approved for continuing employment in fiscal year 2025, accounting for 77.6% of all petitions approved in that category. China was a distant second, with 31,581 petitions, or 10.8%.The deference policy, introduced in 2004, provides a degree of predictability for employers seeking to retain foreign workers. Under the existing approach, officers generally defer to an earlier approval unless there has been a material change in circumstances, a significant error in the earlier decision or new information that adversely affects eligibility.The first Trump administration rescinded the deference policy in 2017, giving officers greater latitude to reassess eligibility with every extension request, even when the underlying facts remained unchanged. This was followed by a significant rise in requests for evidence (RFEs) and denials. The Biden administration reinstated the deference policy in 2021 and codified and expanded it in regulations in late 2024 to provide employers greater predictability. In August 2025, the second Trump administration proposed eliminating the regulation as part of another rulemaking but did not pursue it. The Trump administration’s recent move marks its third attempt to eliminate deference.If the proposed rule is finalised, employers could face more requests for evidence, longer processing times and a higher risk of denials when seeking extensions of stay for H-1B and other temporary work visa holders, explained Wexler.According to Fragomen, following the 2017 rescission of the policy, the H-1B extension denial rate reached 24%, compared with around 3.5% currently; the L-1B denial rate peaked at 35%, against approximately 9% at present.The proposal has heightened anxiety among the Indian diaspora, with the uncertainty extending well beyond the workplace. If an H-1B extension is denied and the worker has no other lawful basis to remain in the US, families could be forced to confront the prospect of leaving behind homes, children’s schools, established careers and community networks built over years. For households with both spouses working or children growing up in the US, the consequences could be particularly disruptive, forcing difficult decisions about whether the entire family relocates or whether family members face a period of separation.You use AI every day. articles.title: I do not have confidence UK is safe from Russian threats - Swinney
articles.summary: The first minister speaks to BBC Scotland News ahead of the SNP's annual conference in Aberdeen.
articles.body:
First Minister John Swinney says he does not have confidence the UK is safe from potential Russian threats.

The SNP leader said the UK government, which is in charge of Britain's defences, did not have a sufficient "presence" in vulnerable areas off Scotland's coast.

He said he was "very worried" by security fears highlighted this week by the head of MI5, Sir Ken McCallum, who named Russia as "aggressor number one".

Speaking to BBC Scotland News ahead of the SNP's annual conference, Swinney also denied that independence would weaken Scotland's security.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said his government is committed to investing in defence, including nuclear deterrence, while not seeking to escalate tensions with Russia.

MI5 chief warns of threats to UK from Russia, Iran and AI

Burnham to visit Scotland during SNP conference

No probe into claims Swinney misled Holyrood

Asked about the MI5 chief's comments, the first minister said he was "very worried" about a "lack of coastal and offshore protection".

He identified waters north of Shetland as an area of significant Russian activity.

"I don't think we've got nearly the presence in those areas that we require today," he told BBC Scotland News.

"There's an obligation on the United Kingdom government to make sure that the country is safe. And I don't think the defence posture of the United Kingdom enables me to have that confidence."

Scotland is home to the UK's nuclear submarine fleet at Faslane, west of Glasgow. The SNP wants those weapons to be removed, but is in favour of an independent Scotland joining Nato.

Swinney insisted that independence would not hamper Scotland's security, but rather give the country "more choices".

The SNP leader said he had "always been a believer in defence co-operation between Scotland and other countries", citing Canada joining the EU's SAFE defence programme .

Responding to the first minister's comments, a Ministry of Defence Spokesperson said:

"The first duty of government is to keep its citizens safe, and this government is investing £298bn over the next four years to ensure we can tackle rising threats.

"The Navy is helping to patrol Nato's northern flank, with this year's carrier strike group deploying to the Arctic and the high north.

"To tackle these threats, we're also investing in new frigates for the Navy and high-tech uncrewed vessels as part of our Hybrid Navy, backed by £1.5bn in funding."

Delivering a speech at the UN General Assembly last month, Burnham said his government would invest in defence and build up the UK's "hard power and deterrence".

He added: "But we will not play Russia's game of trading escalatory rhetoric. Unlike Russia, we do not seek confrontation."

SNP members are gathering in Aberdeen for the party's annual conference, which starts on Thursday and ends with Swinney's keynote speech on Saturday afternoon.

Burnham has also selected this weekend to visit Scotland. He is expected to travel to the central belt to discuss plans to devolve power to local communities.

Swinney, who has invited the Labour leader to the SNP conference, said he had "not yet" accepted the offer.

The first minister welcomed Burnham's recent announcement that he wanted to secure better trade terms with the EU for producers of salmon, shellfish, and seed potatoes.

The prime minister also wants to discuss even closer ties with the bloc and has not ruled out a future referendum on rejoining.

Swinney told the BBC: "I think it's an interesting precedent that if we can reopen an issue that's been decided by a referendum, then we can also reopen Scottish independence."

Ahead of the conference, the SNP announced it would launch a new independence campaign - including a national day of action, digital and broadcast adverts, and an independence survey delivered to almost 1.5m people.

The Scottish government is aiming to hold a second referendum by 2031.

The Supreme Court has ruled that could only happen with Westminster's consent.

Arguing the case for a second vote, Swinney points to the record number of pro-independence MSPs elected to Holyrood in May - though the proportion of pro-independence votes decreased from about 50% to about 41% since 2021.

Burnham said in the Commons last month that a second referendum could be held once there was a clear consensus and public opinion had changed.

However, he later insisted that there was no consensus, adding that such a vote remained "off limits".

Burnham later made a special mention of Swinney In his speech to the Labour Party conference, insisting he was "utterly determined" to prove wrong the SNP leader's prediction that he would be the last prime minister of the UK.

Swinney was also challenged on the preparedness of the NHS for winter pressures after an emergency doctor warned of "unsafe levels of care" and a "toxic normalisation" of corridor care.

Dr Fiona Hunter, vice-chair of the Royal College of Emergency Medicine in Scotland, told BBC Scotland News that she was "completely terrified" of the situation.

The first minister said he could "hear, understand and appreciate" these concerns and accepted that there were "significant challenges" in the system.

However, he said hospital flow plans were designed to reduce pressures and the Scottish government intended to end corridor care "at the earliest possible opportunity".

articles.title: Ukraine's Starlink scare - a cautionary note for India?
articles.summary: TOI Correspondent from Washington: The raging debate in India over Elon Musk’s bid to muscle Starlink into the country has received a cautionary call
articles.body: TOI Correspondent from Washington: The raging debate in India over Elon Musk’s bid to muscle Starlink into the country has received a cautionary call after Ukraine reported on Wednesday that its military units suffered disruptions due to unexpected restrictions on Starlink terminals, affecting high-speed connectivity used in combat missions.Ukrainian officials and commentators are alleging that the Starlink restrictions might be connected to Washington’s pressure on Ukraine to halt strikes against Russian oil infrastructure. “Clearly, this action cannot be a coincidence and is linked to the current political situation,” Serhiy Beskrestnov, a Ukrainian military expert who advises President Volodymyr Zelensky on weapons technologies, wrote on a social media platform, as several US lawmakers and European leaders fumed about President Trump appearing to throw Kyiv under the bus after announcing a deal with Moscow to buy diesel.Starlink, operated by SpaceX (founded by Elon Musk) is a satellite internet constellation that provides high-speed, low-latency broadband internet access in underserved, rural, and remote locations where traditional cable or fiber-optic infrastructure is unavailable or unreliable. Musk and his company SpaceX have rendered matchless service to Ukraine, activating Starlink service to the country within days of the Russian invasion to help hospitals, emergency services and government offices stay connected during the war. By some accounts, Ukraine now has more than 50,000 Starlink terminals.Ukrainian officials are now accusing SpaceX of crippling its drone missions among other effects, although Musk defenders say the restrictions appear to affect only military-grade Starshield, which is operated by the US government and isn't under SpaceX's control. The Trump administration and Starlink have not responded to the charges at the time of writing, but the very possibility illustrates the dilemma facing India of opening itself to a technology controlled by a company – that too owned by a partisan political hack – operating within another country’s political and regulatory system.Starlink has become a particularly contentious issue after Musk accused Indian business interests of blocking its entry to protect their monopolies, implicitly targeting Reliance Jio chairman Mukesh Ambani. New Delhi has rejected the suggestion that its regulatory framework is discriminatory. Starlink has secured important licences and authorisations but is reported to be awaiting security clearances and spectrum assignment before commercial operations can begin.A report titled Starlink and Risks for India from Takshashila Institution, released in April this year, has raised precisely this point: foreign control of connectivity and data security, and the vulnerability that comes from relying on a foreign private operator.Even ahead of Wednesday’s developments, the report had noted that Starlink's service availability had been altered or restricted during conflicts (such as in Ukraine) or used to bypass state blockades during civil unrest (such as in Iran), while warning that a foreign corporate decision, technical failure, or external pressure could disrupt critical communications in India during a crisis.For Kyiv, the timing could hardly be worse. Russia launched scores of ballistic missiles and drone attacks against Ukrainian targets this week, striking energy infrastructure and leaving approximately 600,000 people without electricity. The country is heading into another winter under bombardment, with its air defences under enormous strain, and President Trump transparently intent on turning the screws on Kyiv in an effort to end the war, even if it is in Russia’s terms.You use AI every day.
