articles.title: A UK civil servant, Kashim Chowdhury, allegedly juggled five full-time government jobs, earned £349,378 across eight roles between 2020 and 2023, and was contracted to work 183 hours a week
articles.summary: A UK civil servant accused of earning £349,378 across eight government jobs allegedly attended virtual meetings with his camera switched off, citing
articles.body: A UK civil servant accused of earning £349,378 across eight government jobs allegedly attended virtual meetings with his camera switched off, citing technical problems, a court has heard. According to a report by Personnel Today, Kashim Chowdhury, 55, is accused of lying to secure positions across several government departments and public bodies, including the Food Standards Agency, the Home Office and the Department for Business and Trade. He denies nine counts of fraud.Prosecutors told Southwark Crown Court that Chowdhury held eight different jobs between February 2020 and September 2023, earning £349,378 before the alleged fraud was discovered.At the peak of his employment, he allegedly held five full-time positions simultaneously and was contracted to work 183 hours a week.Prosecutor Lucy Organ told the court, “That is more hours than there are in a week if he didn't sleep at all, and worked night and day every day of the week.”When his employers reportedly began to grow suspicious, Chowdhury allegedly claimed he was unwell. On one occasion, he is said to have appeared in an online meeting with white make-up smeared across his face, jurors were told.Manager describes Chowdhury's work as ineffectiveThe court also heard testimony from Dan McCartney, Chowdhury's former line manager at the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), where he was employed on an annual salary of £52,000.McCartney told the court that he believed Chowdhury was close to requiring a formal performance management review.“He was pretty close to needing them,” he said.Asked by Organ whether Chowdhury's work had ever improved, McCartney replied, “No.”The manager said he had to monitor Chowdhury's work “much more than I would expect to do for someone of his grade”.“I had to tell him what to do. I would have expected him to be self-sufficient,” he added.McCartney also told the court that he had disagreed with the decision to make Chowdhury a permanent employee. He explained that, under the department's policy, employees on fixed-term contracts could be made permanent if they were not subject to performance management measures.“I wasn't in agreement with it but I was told that it was something that would have to happen,” he said.Court hears about camera-off meetings and alleged IT problemsMcCartney said Chowdhury regularly attended virtual meetings with his camera switched off. He told the court that he had asked him to resolve the issue, as he considered it important for team members to have their cameras on during meetings.“He said he had IT problems with his laptop and I asked him to resolve it so that the camera worked,” McCartney said.He added that it took several months of repeated requests before the issue was resolved.Organ also asked McCartney whether Chowdhury had ever disclosed that he was working elsewhere while employed at Defra.“No,” the former manager replied.Chowdhury denies nine counts of fraudThe court heard that Chowdhury, who lives in Whitechapel, east London, had told his employers that he was struggling with his work because his mother had been diagnosed with cancer.Chowdhury denies nine counts of fraud. articles.title: US drops case against ex-CIA analyst accused of working for South Korea in exchange for luxury gifts
articles.summary: The US Justice Department has suspended charges against ex-CIA analyst Sue Mi Terry, accused of working for South Korea in exchange for luxury gifts. The case will be deferred for 12 months under specific conditions, avoiding an immediate trial.
articles.body: The US Justice Department has agreed to drop criminal charges against former CIA analyst Sue Mi Terry, who was accused of secretly working for South Korea’s government in exchange for luxury goods and other gifts.Under an agreement filed in a Manhattan federal court on Tuesday, prosecutors will suspend the case for 12 months. If Terry follows the conditions set out in the deal, the charges against her will be dropped at the end of that period.The agreement comes weeks before the case was due to go to trial, according to The New York Times. It means Terry will not face an immediate criminal conviction or prison sentence.Terry, a former White House National Security Council official, was indicted in July 2024. Prosecutors accused her of accepting gifts from South Korean officials in return for promoting Seoul’s policy positions, sharing information that was not publicly available and helping South Korean officials gain access to their American counterparts.The allegations relate to activities that prosecutors said began in 2013, two years after Terry left US government service, and continued for about a decade. During that period, she worked as a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, where she focused on East Asia and the Korean Peninsula.The indictment accused Terry of failing to register as a foreign agent under US law and conspiring to violate the Foreign Agents Registration Act, which requires people carrying out certain political activities on behalf of foreign governments to disclose that work.The Justice Department did not explain why it had agreed to suspend the case. The four-page notice said prosecutors had determined that “the interests of the United States and your own interest will be best served by deferring prosecution”.Under the deal, Terry must follow several conditions, including restrictions on her travel and contact with the South Korean government. She has not admitted to wrongdoing as part of the agreement, although she acknowledged helping South Korean intelligence officers in several ways.One example involved notes she had prepared for a 2022 meeting between senior US State Department officials and experts on Korean policy. Under the agreement, she acknowledged sharing those notes with South Korean intelligence officers.Terry has denied the allegations. Her lawyer, Lee Wolosky, previously argued that she was being prosecuted for work carried out as an independent academic and news analyst. He also said she had been a strong critic of the South Korean government.“We have consistently maintained that her interactions with South Korean officials were conducted in furtherance of US interests and her work as a leading American specialist on North Korea and East Asia,” Wolosky said in a statement about the agreement, as quoted by The New York Times.Terry was placed on unpaid leave by the Council on Foreign Relations after her indictment.You use AI every day. articles.title: An Ohio company paid $12,100 for Cleveland land and put $40,000 into a planned used-car lot; months later the city rezoned it residential, and an appeals court said the move was a compensable taking
articles.summary: An Ohio appeals court has ruled that the City of Cleveland must begin compensation proceedings after changing the zoning of a commercial property to
articles.body: An Ohio appeals court has ruled that the City of Cleveland must begin compensation proceedings after changing the zoning of a commercial property to residential use, preventing the owner from carrying out a planned business project. The Court of Appeals of Ohio, Eighth Appellate District, upheld a lower court ruling that requires the city to start formal proceedings to determine compensation for the landowner, TMS Enterprises, Ltd. The dispute began after the company spent thousands of dollars preparing a site for a used-car dealership, only for the city to change the property's zoning to residential use months later.Purchase and initial site investmentCourt documents show that TMS Enterprises bought a parcel of land in Cleveland for $12,100, intending to open a used-car dealership. After purchasing the property, the company spent another $40,000 preparing the site for the planned business. The investment was based on the expectation that the land could be used for commercial purposes. However, months after the company made these investments, the City of Cleveland changed the zoning rules for the property. The land was moved from a commercial or retail classification to a residential zone. This change prevented the company from operating a vehicle sales business on the site and stopped it from using the property for its intended commercial purpose.Legal struggle over property rightsFaced with the new restrictions, TMS Enterprises took the matter to court. The company argued that the city's decision had made its investments useless and amounted to an unconstitutional taking of private property through government regulation. Article I, Section 19 of the Ohio Constitution and the Fifth Amendment to the United States Constitution protect private property rights. They state that private property cannot be taken for public use without fair compensation. When government rules place severe limits on how land can be used, property owners may file an inverse condemnation claim. This legal action asks a court to require the government to begin formal appropriation proceedings and determine how much compensation the owner should receive. The City of Cleveland disputed the company's claim. It argued that the zoning changes did not amount to a regulatory taking that required compensation.Appeals panel upholds rulingIn TMS Enterprises, Ltd. v. Cleveland, the Eighth District Court of Appeals upheld the lower court's decision in favour of the landowner. The appeals court reviewed the effects of the zoning change under established legal standards, including the test set out by the United States Supreme Court in Penn Central Transportation Co. v. New York City. The appellate panel concluded that the city's sudden zoning change had gone far enough to qualify as a compensable regulatory taking. The court found that the change caused serious financial harm to the company and interfered with its reasonable expectations for the property, based on the money it had invested. TMS Enterprises had bought the land and spent $40,000 preparing it for commercial use before the city changed the zoning rules. These steps showed that the company had made specific plans for a used-car dealership. The new residential classification prevented those plans from going ahead. As a result of the appeals court's decision, the City of Cleveland must now move forward with formal appropriation proceedings. During this process, a jury or court magistrate will determine the amount of compensation owed to TMS Enterprises for the loss of the property's intended use and the financial value affected by the zoning change.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2017, Randy Orton and Bray Wyatt turned a run-down Missouri home into WWE’s “House of Horrors”; the two-bedroom house on three acres was already listed for just $36,000
articles.summary: Discover how a rundown Missouri house was transformed into WWE’s House of Horrors, hosting the eerie showdown between Randy Orton and Bray Wyatt. This two-bedroom, $36,000 fixer-upper captured wrestling fans' attention and added unexpected fame to an overlooked property.
articles.body: In professional wrestling, a house can become part of the spectacle as much as the ring itself. That was the case in 2017, when WWE turned a run-down property in Missouri into the setting for a bizarre showdown between Randy Orton and Bray Wyatt. According to Realtor.com, the two-bedroom, one-bathroom house in Richmond, Missouri, had been on the property market for about three years by May 2017, with its original asking price of $69,900 reduced to just $36,000. Set on approximately three acres, the property was being sold as a fixer-upper, with considerable renovation work likely to be needed.The listing described the house as being sold “as is”, while the listing broker noted that it remained in rough condition and had water in the basement. Its appearance in WWE’s House of Horrors match between Randy Orton and Bray Wyatt brought unexpected attention to a property that had struggled to find a buyer, turning an ordinary real estate listing into a talking point among wrestling fans.A wrestling match that began inside a real houseThe unusual property featured in WWE’s House of Horrors match at Payback on 30 April 2017. The storyline pitted Orton against Wyatt in a horror-themed match at the house. According to WWE, the contest began at the house before moving to the SAP Centre in San Jose, California, where the wrestlers continued in front of the live audience. The filmed sequence showed Orton entering the dimly lit property, searching for Wyatt and being ambushed as the action moved through different rooms. The kitchen became one of the most memorable scenes when Wyatt tipped a refrigerator onto Orton before leaving the house.With dark interiors, disturbing décor, and a well-planned scene, an ordinary residential building became a battlefield on stage. The film segment also managed to create a geographic illusion, with the house segment becoming part of an event happening in California while it was actually located in Missouri. The address was quickly found out by wrestling fans, who found that the house was located in Richmond, Missouri. Accounts at the time said the house was along Business 10 Highway, about an hour from Kansas City, not in San Jose. This revelation gave the property a second life online as fans shared the listing.A fixer-upper with a low asking priceAway from the extravagant presentation by WWE, the property was being marketed as a renovation project. Realtor.com described it as a two-bedroom, one-bathroom house that needed considerable work, with the sale offered on an “as is” basis. By May 2017, the asking price had fallen from $69,900 to $36,000, reflecting the challenges of selling a property in rough condition. The house had reportedly been on the market for about three years before its appearance in the wrestling match, making its low asking price and neglected state an important part of the story behind the televised spectacle.According to Adkins, stage props were used during the production, and the property emerged in good condition. However, real estate broker Wendy Flynn noted that the extent of any structural damage was difficult to assess. The two accounts suggest a distinction between the visible destruction shown on screen and the condition of the building itself. Although furniture was toppled and a refrigerator crashed down on Randy Orton, these staged scenes did not necessarily mean the house had sustained comparable structural damage. Without a clear assessment of the building, its condition after filming could not be established solely from what viewers saw.How a low-value property became a wrestling curiosityThe house’s sudden fame showed how a brief television appearance could draw attention to a property that was struggling to attract buyers. The property quickly drew attention from wrestling fans because of its price, location, and condition. Nevertheless, the extra attention did not solve the practical problems associated with the purchase of the house. Though it offered plenty of space, the need for renovation and reports of basement flooding made a buyer inspection essential. Flynn stated in the Realtor.com report that a home inspection was essential for a potential buyer.Another question the property raised was whether its fame could be turned into money-making opportunities. Flynn joked that someone looking to make a quick buck could buy the property and charge people to see it. This was not necessarily a plan, but it highlighted the unique commercial value the event created for the property. In the end, there were two reasons the Missouri property became famous. First, for WWE fans, it was the eerie location where Orton and Wyatt met. For potential buyers, it was simply a modest property with land and a few issues, priced at $36,000.You use AI every day. articles.body: Washington education officials called a teenage wrestler’s asserted need for emergency Supreme Court relief "manufactured," urging the justices to reject her request to avoid competing against transgender opponents after she alleged she was sexually assaulted by one during a match. Attorneys for the Office of Superintendent of Public Instruction and Superintendent Chris Reykdal argued that the family had not established a likelihood of future injury requiring immediate intervention. "The ‘irreparable’ nature of Applicants’ claimed harm is manufactured," the state’s filing said. "Applicants have sought emergency relief three times despite there not being any true emergency." WASHINGTON FAMILY REQUESTS SCOTUS INJUNCTION AFTER DAUGHTER WAS ALLEGEDLY SEXUALLY ASSAULTED BY TRANS ATHLETE The accusation concerned the family’s claim of future irreparable harm and the need for immediate court intervention. The state’s response was one of three oppositions filed Tuesday in the case brought by Kallie Keeler, identified in court as K.M.K., and her mother, Stephanie Lynne Brown. Puyallup School District and the Washington Interscholastic Activities Association also asked the Supreme Court to deny relief. Keeler alleges a transgender opponent sexually assaulted her during a December 2025 girls’ wrestling match. Her family is seeking an injunction allowing her to return to wrestling without being matched against a male athlete, or protections allowing advance notice and an opportunity to opt out without penalty. A district judge denied a preliminary injunction Aug. 23, and the Ninth Circuit denied emergency relief Sept. 25. The Supreme Court had not ruled on the application as of Tuesday evening. FEMALE WRESTLER WHO WAS ALLEGEDLY SEXUALLY ASSAULTED BY TRANS ATHLETE OPENS UP ON WAGING TITLE IX LAWSUIT The state’s attorneys pointed to the approximately six months between the match and the lawsuit, followed by another month before the family sought a preliminary injunction. They also argued the family’s asserted urgency shifted from the start of soccer season to the school year and then wrestling season, which begins in mid-November. ADF senior counsel Hal Frampton previously told OutKick that Supreme Court intervention was necessary to secure protection before Keeler’s remaining high school seasons slip away. "Our only avenue for relief in advance of wrestling season is the Supreme Court," Frampton said. The state also invoked an upcoming ballot measure as a reason for the justices to refrain from intervening. Washington voters will consider Initiative IL26-638 on Nov. 3. The measure would prohibit students it defines as biologically male from competing in designated female school athletic competitions and require healthcare providers to verify participants’ biological sex. Separately, the state disputed the family’s parental-rights theory, arguing it would improperly allow parents to dictate rules for school athletics. "But the Constitution does not entitle parents to bespoke athletic rules," its attorneys wrote. Puyallup School District defended its response to Keeler and disputed the premise that it had failed to offer accommodations. Frampton previously accused officials of making "no effort to compromise." The district’s filing cited a separate testing room, counseling offers, an independent investigation and expedited approval of Keeler’s transfer to Puyallup High School. "It has provided all the relief it can," the district’s attorneys wrote. The district said its Title IX investigation of the alleged assault remained ongoing and unresolved. Pierce County prosecutors previously declined to charge Keeler’s opponent, citing their inability to prove third-degree rape beyond a reasonable doubt or overcome a consent defense under case law governing athletic contests. The district also emphasized that Keeler could decline matches without additional consequences imposed by the district. That assurance does not eliminate a recorded forfeit or loss under National Federation of State High School Associations wrestling rules. The distinction is central to the dispute: Keeler’s family seeks to avoid competitive penalties as well as district-imposed consequences. The district argued it cannot change national wrestling rules, control every tournament bracket or provide notice identifying another student’s transgender status. The Wisconsin Interscholastic Athletic Association (WIAA) offered a separate threshold defense, arguing Title IX does not apply to it because it is a private nonprofit association that receives no federal funding. The association cited the Supreme Court’s 1999 NCAA v. Smith decision, which held that dues from federally funded members did not make the NCAA a recipient of federal financial assistance. Keeler’s attorneys have advanced a separate theory that the WIAA exercises controlling authority over federally funded schools’ athletic programs. The WIAA disputed that theory and argued it required further factual development. The association also said Keeler had not applied for a hardship waiver concerning varsity eligibility following her transfer. That waiver process concerns transfer eligibility; it does not itself provide the assurance against transgender matchups sought in the emergency application. On forfeits, the WIAA argued that its rules allowing additional penalties for certain withdrawals apply to postseason competition and that any such penalty is discretionary. It said no penalty had been imposed on Keeler and its board had not been asked to consider her circumstances. The association maintained that the requested injunction would require information and operational control it lacks. "An injunction a defendant cannot obey is not a remedy; it is a contempt trap," its attorneys wrote. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! All three responses emphasized that the Supreme Court’s recent West Virginia v. B.P.J. ruling permitted sex-based restrictions but left unresolved whether Title IX prohibits schools from allowing transgender girls onto girls’ teams. The family’s application also asks the Supreme Court to take up the case before the Ninth Circuit finishes its review. The defendants urged the justices to let proceedings continue in the lower courts. articles.title: Shania Twain went to school hungry as a child; after launching Shania Kids Can in 2010, she helped bring school-based support to vulnerable children, including a clubhouse in North Las Vegas
articles.summary: Shania Twain has often spoken about the childhood experiences that shaped her, including going to school without breakfast or lunch.
articles.body: Shania Twain has often spoken about the childhood experiences that shaped her, including going to school without breakfast or lunch. In 2010, she turned that memory into action by founding Shania Kids Can, a school-based programme created to support vulnerable children through food assistance, academic help, one-on-one guidance, and a safe place to belong. According to the Shania Twain Foundation, Twain has said that hunger left her without energy, enthusiasm, or motivation to interact with others during her school years.The organisation, now part of the Shania Twain Foundation, focuses on food insecurity, youth empowerment, and mental wellbeing. Its work includes a Shania Kids Can Clubhouse at Martin Luther King Jr. Elementary School in North Las Vegas, created through a partnership with Communities In Schools of Southern Nevada. The programme gives children a consistent, supportive environment where they can receive practical help and emotional support during the school day.A childhood that shaped the missionTwain has described how food insecurity affected not only her body, but also her ability to learn and connect with classmates. She wrote on the foundation’s website that hunger caused a lack of energy and made it harder to feel enthusiastic or motivated at school. She also recalled feeling different from peers who arrived with cleaner clothes, freshly washed and brushed hair, healthy teeth, and appropriate lunches. Those everyday differences can affect a child’s confidence and sense of belonging, especially when they are already dealing with instability at home.Twain has said, on her foundation's website, that she would have benefited from having even one person guide her through those difficult years. That personal reflection became a central idea behind Shania Kids Can: children need more than material support, and they also need adults who see them, listen to them, and believe in them.Shania Kids Can was founded in 2010Shania Kids Can was founded in 2010 to address the needs of children whose difficulties at home or in their communities were affecting their education, self-esteem, and wellbeing. The Canadian Encyclopedia notes that the organisation provides schools with food, nutritional supplies, recreational equipment, and access to music lessons for underprivileged children.The programme’s approach is built around “wrap-around” support. Rather than focusing on a single issue, it combines academic assistance, social and emotional learning, group activities, and access to nutritious snacks or meals where needed.The foundation says Shania Kids Can has provided localised programming within schools since 2010 to reduce the daily effects of poverty and hunger. Its broader goal is to reach more children and families across North America through partnerships, funding, and grants for under-resourced organisations.The clubhouse modelA defining feature of the programme is the Shania Kids Can Clubhouse. It is designed as a safe, confidence-building space within a school where children know they can go for help every day.Inside the clubhouse, trained programme leaders work with children through one-on-one consultations, academic support, and group activities. The setting is intended to give students a sense of stability while also helping them develop social and emotional skills.The model recognises that a child’s ability to learn is closely connected to how safe, fed, and emotionally supported they feel. When basic needs are met, children are better able to concentrate, participate, and build positive relationships with teachers and classmates.Bringing the programme to North Las VegasIn 2013, Twain helped bring a Shania Kids Can Clubhouse to North Las Vegas. Vegas Inc reported that the programme was launched at Martin Luther King Jr. Elementary School, giving students access to a dedicated support space within their school community.The North Las Vegas clubhouse was established through a partnership with Communities In Schools of Southern Nevada. The collaboration allowed the programme to connect with local school staff and community resources, making the support more responsive to students’ needs.For children facing economic hardship or family instability, the clubhouse offered something practical and consistent. It was a place where they could receive food support, academic help, and guidance from adults who understood the importance of building trust over time.Food, confidence, and mental healthThe Shania Twain Foundation describes food stability as a foundation for children’s physical and mental functioning. It affects concentration, memory, mood, and motor skills, all of which influence how children learn and participate in school.Twain’s own experience also informs the foundation’s mental health focus. She has written that she sometimes stayed home from school to avoid discomfort, and that she forged absence notes to protect her family’s privacy. She described the stress of carrying that burden alone as a child.That perspective helps explain why the programme treats emotional wellbeing as inseparable from academic support. Depression, anger, bullying, and isolation can be signs that a child is struggling to survive emotionally, and the foundation says its work aims to help children develop a positive self-image regardless of their circumstances.Why the work still mattersChildhood hunger and poverty remain major barriers to education. A child who arrives at school hungry may struggle to focus, withdraw from classmates, or fall behind academically, even when they are capable of succeeding with the right support. Twain’s foundation frames food stability as a basic condition for learning, not an extra benefit.Shania Kids Can’s school-based model is important because it meets children where they already are. Instead of requiring families to seek help elsewhere, the programme brings support into the school environment, where children spend much of their day.Twain’s story also shows how personal hardship can become a source of purpose. By creating spaces where children feel seen, fed, and supported, she has turned a painful childhood memory into a practical effort to help young people avoid some of the isolation and shame she once experienced.From one singer’s promise to a wider foundationShania Kids Can began as a focused charity for vulnerable schoolchildren, but it has since evolved into the Shania Twain Foundation. The foundation now aims to expand its reach through strategic partnerships and grants that support organisations working with vulnerable communities across North America.The core mission has remained consistent: help children facing poverty, hunger, and emotional distress feel safe, capable, and supported. The foundation says children who receive care and stability often respond by showing the same care to others, creating a ripple effect beyond the classroom.For Twain, the work is deeply personal. Her experience of going to school hungry did not define her future, but it gave her a clear understanding of what children need when life at home is difficult. Through Shania Kids Can and the foundation that grew from it, she has worked to ensure that more children have access to the support she once wished she had.You use AI every day. articles.title: Eligibility alone will decide allocation of flats in Indiramma towers, says Ponguleti
articles.summary: Telangana minister Ponguleti says Indiramma tower flats will be allotted solely on eligibility, not politics; 480 beneficiaries picked via draw at Pocharam.
articles.body: Hyderabad: The Telangana govt would ensure equal development across all constituencies, irrespective of whether they were represented by ruling Congress or opposition parties, revenue and housing minister Ponguleti Srinivas Reddy said on Wednesday.Eligibility alone would determine the allocation of Indiramma houses, with no room for political considerations, he said.Speaking after laying the foundation stone for Indiramma housing towers at Pocharam in Medchal-Malkajgiri district, along with industries and IT minister Duddilla Sridhar Babu, MP Eatela Rajender, MLA Ch Malla Reddy and MLC P Mahender Reddy, Ponguleti said the govt was committed to providing dignified housing to the urban poor in the areas where they currently lived.“The Congress govt is trying to end the practice of shifting urban poor to distant locations outside the city, which used to affect their livelihoods and employment opportunities. The first phase of Indiramma housing scheme in the CURE area aims to construct one lakh houses in a phased manner, with the tender process completed for works in 23 constituencies so far. Foundation stones have already been laid at six locations,” he said.The minister said 480 beneficiaries in Medchal constituency were selected through a transparent public draw after online applications were scrutinised and eligibility verified. The LIG flats were being allotted only to eligible local residents who did not already own homes.He said 4.50 lakh Indiramma houses had been sanctioned in the first phase in rural areas, with financial assistance of ₹5 lakh for each house. Construction of more than 2.20 lakh houses had been completed so far, while another 2.50 lakh houses had been sanctioned in the second phase in rural areas. Applications for the second phase of Indiramma towers in the CURE area would be invited soon, he added.Ponguleti said selected beneficiaries of the towers would receive registered ownership of their flats, including the associated land share, without registration charges. The govt aimed to complete the flats and hand over keys to first-phase beneficiaries by the Bathukamma festival next year.He assured those who missed out in the first phase that eligible applicants, including new applicants, would be considered in subsequent phases. He also directed officials to complete unfinished double-bedroom houses constructed during the previous BRS govt tenure and allot vacant units to eligible poor families. articles.summary: Chandigarh State Election Commission appoints ROs and AROs for all 35 MC wards ahead of general elections; nine officers assigned ward groups, with reserves named.
articles.body: Chandigarh: The Chandigarh State Election Commission has appointed returning officers (ROs) and assistant returning officers (AROs) for all 35 MC wards ahead of the forthcoming general election.State election commissioner Vijay Dev issued the notifications on Oct 13 in consultation with the Chandigarh administration. The appointments cover electoral registration and scrutiny responsibilities, along with the conduct of the ward-level election process.Under the notification, nine officers have been appointed as electoral registration officers and returning officers/scrutinising officers for groups of wards.Pradhuman Singh, additional excise and taxation commissioner/collector (excise), has been assigned wards 1 to 4, while Nitish Singla, director, school education, will oversee wards 5 to 8.Palika Arora, director, technical education, has been assigned wards 9 to 12, while Naveen, DANICS, chief general manager of CITCO, has been assigned wards 13 to 16. articles.title: Residents living near Jantar Mantar hope for quieter mornings
articles.summary: Residents near Delhi’s Jantar Mantar hope de-notification as a protest site will reduce noise, crowds and security restrictions disrupting daily life.
articles.body: NNew Delhi: Some people wake up to alarm clocks. Others wake up to birdsong. For residents near Jantar Mantar, the morning soundtrack in recent months has often been protest slogans, loudspeakers and the movement of security personnel. A trip to the office, a run to buy rations or even a quick dash to the neighbourhood shop could come with an unexpected obstacle course.With Jantar Mantar being de-notified as a designated protest site, residents are hoping the change will turn down the volume on their daily lives.“You see that road? There are security forces everywhere, and restrictions make even the simplest things difficult,” said David, a resident of the area. “Whether it is getting ration or stepping out for some work, everything becomes a task. Even crossing the area feels like navigating a maze.”For David, the announcement is a reason to hope, but not yet a reason to relax. “We are hearing that things have changed, so let’s see what happens next,” he said, hoping residents would finally be able to go about their daily lives without having to plan every little errand around security arrangements.Sushil Yadav, who has lived in the area for nearly 50 years, said the disruption would sometimes reach right up to residents’ doorsteps. Recalling the situation in July, he said people had come close to residential lanes, with some asking for water and others seeking access to toilets.“There were all sorts of requests. But how can we let everyone into our homes?” he said. “In such situations, everything in our lane would get restricted, and it felt as though we were locked inside our own houses.”Yadav said he is not asking for people to stop protesting, but wants a place where they can make their voices heard without turning residents’ everyday lives upside down. “Having a designated place for protests, where people can gather without disturbing our daily lives, would work much better,” he said.For Mark, who has fixed office timings to stick to, crowds and noise are more than a passing annoyance; they can make an ordinary commute stressful.“When there is no metro service nearby, travelling becomes even more difficult. On top of that, there is so much crowd and noise. It gets overwhelming and irritating when you are simply trying to get to work,” he said. “Let’s hope the nearby areas are not affected this time.”Akanksha, another resident, said even a quick trip to buy chips for her daughter came with the familiar worry of getting around amid the disruption. With her daughter’s school closed, travelling with her could be chaotic, she said, adding the noise sometimes made matters worse.For some, the move means no more turning a short errand into a logistical exercise, no more feeling boxed in by restrictions and no more wondering what awaits outside the front door. articles.title: Dipke asks supporters to gather at CP to wave Tricolour
articles.summary: Abhijit Dipke urges supporters to gather at Connaught Place’s Central Park and wave the Tricolour, condemning arrests of CJP members in Delhi.
articles.body: New Delhi: Abhijit Dipke, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder, landed in Delhi Wednesdasy and called on all his supporters to gather at Central Park in Connaught Place Friday with the Tricolour.“Waving our national flag is a fundamental expression of our patriotism, not a criminal act,” Dipke said in a video message. “The state’s heavy-handed crackdown on dissent will not silence people. I urge every citizen who believes in democratic rights to reach Central Park this Friday, carrying the Tricolour. If the administration wants to arrest peaceful citizens simply for holding the national flag, let them prepare their jails,” he said.Hours before, in Nagpur, Dipke said the arrest of his associates, Saurabh Das and Ashutosh Ranka, was an attempt by govt to impose an undeclared Emergency in the country. “I want to tell Narendra Modi, if you want to clamp Emergency, then have the guts to make it official. Why are you enforcing an unofficial Emergency by detaining people for five days just for waving the Tricolour at Jantar Mantar?” he asked.He was referring to the arrests of the CJP members.
